subject: Banking
title: Long-Term Capital Management
description: A quick win: understand Long-Term Capital Management.

hook.text: LTCM was run by Nobel Prize winners. Their hedge fund nearly crashed the global financial system in 1998.

buildup.text: LTCM used mathematical models to find tiny price differences in bond markets.

discovery.text: Russia's debt default in 1998 caused market turmoil their models didn't predict. LTCM lost $4.6 billion in four months.

twist.text: The Fed organized a $3.6 billion rescue by 14 banks. Taxpayer money wasn't used.

climax.text: Nobel Prize models failed because markets aren't purely mathematical.

punchline.text: Nobel Prize winners. 25:1 leverage. $4.6 billion lost in four months.

quiz.question: Why did LTCM's models fail?
options: They couldn't account for extreme events like Russia's default

details.summary: Long-Term Capital Management was a hedge fund run by Nobel laureates that used extreme leverage to make bets on bond markets. When Russia defaulted in 1998, LTCM's $4.6 billion in losses threatened to cascade through the entire financial system.
details.whyItMatters: LTCM proved that genius does not eliminate risk. Its near-failure showed how a single leveraged fund could threaten systemic stability, foreshadowing the too-big-to-fail problems of 2008.
takeaways: LTCM leveraged $4 billion in capital into $125 billion in positions
Two Nobel Prize-winning economists designed its trading strategies
The Fed organized a $3.6 billion private-sector rescue to prevent contagion

faq.question: How did Nobel Prize winners lose so much money?
faq.answer: LTCM's models assumed historical patterns would continue and markets would remain liquid. Russia's unexpected default and subsequent global panic created conditions their models had said were virtually impossible, proving that tail risks can overwhelm any model.

faq.question: Why did the Fed intervene for a private hedge fund?
faq.answer: LTCM's positions were so large and so interconnected with major banks that its uncontrolled collapse would have forced fire sales across global markets. The Fed organized a private rescue rather than a taxpayer bailout to prevent systemic contagion.
